title: List all possible outcomes of a single event

lesson.title: What Could Happen? Listing All the Outcomes

steps.say: You already know how to look at a spinner and guess which colour it will probably land on. Today we do something a little different, and a little easier: instead of guessing which one wins, we just make a list of every single thing that could happen. That list has a name — the possible outcomes.

Look at this spinner from the school fun fair. It has four equal parts: red, blue, green and yellow. If I spin it once, the arrow has to stop somewhere. It could land on red, or on blue, or on green, or on yellow. That is the whole list. So the possible outcomes are red, blue, green, yellow — four outcomes. Notice I did not say which one will win. Listing outcomes just means naming everything that is allowed to happen.

visual.caption: Possible outcomes: red, blue, green, yellow

steps.say: Now here is the interesting part. In my backpack I have a bag of little bouncy balls from the corner store: three red, two white and one green. That is six balls in the bag. I close my eyes and pull out one ball. What could happen? I could pull out a red one, a white one, or a green one. So there are only three possible outcomes, even though there are six balls. Outcomes are the different kinds of results, not the number of objects.

visual.caption: Six balls in the bag, but only three different colours

steps.say: A lot of kids write the list like this: red, red, red, white, white, green — six outcomes. But think about it. If I pull out a red ball, does it matter which red one it was? No. To my eyes it is just red. So red only goes on the list one time. The three reds do change how likely red is, but they do not make new outcomes. The correct list is red, white, green — three outcomes.

visual.caption: Three outcomes; the numbers only tell us how many of each

steps.say: So whenever someone asks you to list the possible outcomes of one spin, one roll, or one draw, just ask yourself: what are all the different results I could see? Name each different one once, and you are done.

lesson.answer: Possible outcomes are all the different results that could happen — name each different one exactly once.

practice.question: At a Richmond night market, a prize spinner is split into six equal parts. Two parts say maple candy, two parts say bubble tea, one part says a two dollar coin, and one part says try again. You may draw this spinner on your paper. If you spin it one time, list all the possible outcomes. How many are there?
practice.answer: The possible outcomes are maple candy, bubble tea, a two dollar coin, and try again — four possible outcomes. (There are six parts, but only four different results, so maple candy and bubble tea each get written just once.)
